headline_marked: Former OSRS dev [[gets jail time for stealing $400,000]] from players in virtual gold scam
headline: Former OSRS dev gets jail time for stealing $400,000 from players in virtual gold scam
summary: Andrew Lakeman, known as 'Mod Jed', stole virtual gold and items from Old School RuneScape accounts, selling them on the black market. Jagex used hidden firewall tweaks to track him down.
details: A former Jagex employee, Andrew Lakeman (aka Mod Jed), has been sentenced to a three-year prison term, suspended for two years, after being found guilty of stealing over $400,000 worth of virtual gold from Old School RuneScape players. He then sold these in-game assets on the black market.

Jagex began investigating in 2018 after noticing a pattern of suspicious account recoveries followed by the disappearance of valuable in-game items and gold. The OSRS economy allows players to trade items and gold, which hold real monetary value.

Initially suspecting a glitch, a deeper investigation led Jagex to believe it was an inside job. To catch the culprit, the company secretly modified its firewall to track illegal activity without alerting its employees.

These measures successfully traced the thefts back to Lakeman, who denied the accusations, claiming his account was hacked. Jagex fired him and reported the incident to the police, who later confirmed the virtual goods were sold for over $400,000.

Lakeman was arrested in July 2019 and sentenced on September 3, receiving a three-year sentence suspended for two years, 150 hours of unpaid work, and 25 days of rehabilitation. Detective Constable Andrew McKeane stated, "Just because it’s virtual, doesn’t mean he shouldn’t face the full force of the law."

headline_marked: [[Cyborg cockroaches could save your life]], delivering first aid in disaster zones
headline: Cyborg cockroaches could save your life, delivering first aid in disaster zones
summary: Researchers developed "Paraborg" cyborg cockroaches that can carry cameras or administer medication, potentially acting as first responders in collapsed buildings.
details: Small robots and drones help in disasters, but new research shows how cyborg bugs, called 'Paraborgs', can go further. Developed by the University of Queensland and UNSW, these giant burrowing cockroaches (up to 87mm, 40g) are designed for both search and first aid missions.

Two types of Paraborgs exist: one with a camera to film victims, and another with an automatic injection mechanism for medication. Cockroaches can carry up to 1.5 times their body weight; the injection unit added 15mm height and 17g, without significantly impairing movement.

The cyborgs are remotely controlled via electrical stimuli to electrodes on their antennae and cerci. Researchers steer the bug by stimulating antennae and control pace by stimulating both cerci, using frequencies between 10 and 40 hertz.
The injection mechanism uses a spring system to deploy a syringe. A chemical reaction between citric acid and baking soda generates carbon dioxide, pushing the plunger to administer medication.

In tests, the Paraborg achieved a 95% success rate for injections within 150mm of a target, and a 72% success rate for the entire sequence from departure to injection. The team also demonstrated successful teamwork between camera and injector cockroaches.

While promising, the experiments did not fully replicate complex disaster environments like debris or uneven terrain. Researchers hope to deploy these cyborg insect rescue teams within 5 to 10 years, leveraging insects' natural strengths for diverse missions.
